note: Beginner on-ramp lessons for criminal procedure and property. These sit below the existing lessons in both modules: they assume no legal training and lead into the harder treatment. Every lesson carries its sources and a `verify` line — the app states a rule, it does not vouch for it.

lessons.title: When the police stop you
lessons.summary: What turns a stop into an arrest, the three things you can ask for, and the clock that starts the moment you are no longer free to go.

sections.keypoint: Most people will never read a contract in a courtroom; many will meet a police officer.

body.text: Most people will never read a contract in a court room. Many will meet a police officer. This lesson is about that meeting, in the order it happens.
It is written for the person it happens to, and for the family at home waiting for news. You need no legal training to follow it.

sections.keypoint: Being stopped and questioned is not an arrest — an arrest is when you are no longer free to leave.

body.text: Faizal drives a lorry in Ipoh. One night the police stop him at a roadblock. They ask for his identity card and look in the cab.
Nothing has happened to Faizal in law yet. He has been stopped and questioned. When the officers finish, he drives away.
Being stopped and questioned is not an arrest. An arrest is the point at which a person is taken into custody and is no longer free to leave.
The line is drawn by control, not by words. Nobody has to say the word arrest. If you are cuffed, held, or put in a vehicle, you are under arrest whatever it is called.

body.title: The one question that tells you which it is
body.caption: Nobody has to say the word arrest. The line is drawn by control. If you are cuffed, held, or put in a vehicle, you are under arrest whatever anyone calls it.
body.alt: A question — are you free to walk away? — branching two ways. Yes: you have been stopped and questioned, and in law nothing has happened to you yet. No, because you are cuffed, held or put in a vehicle: you are under arrest, and the protections that follow an arrest apply.
body.question: Are you free to walk away?

branches.label: Stopped and questioned
branches.note: in law, nothing has happened yet

sections.keypoint: For a seizable offence police may arrest without a warrant; otherwise one is generally needed.

body.text: An arrest takes away your liberty. The officer takes you into custody, either by touching you or because you submit and go along.
For a seizable offence a police officer may arrest without a warrant. For other offences a warrant or an order is generally needed.
A seizable offence is simply one the Code marks for arrest without a warrant. Which offences those are is looked up in the First Schedule, not worked out by argument.

Two neighbours fight outside a kedai runcit. One is arrested at the scene. The other is told to come to the station on Friday. The difference is how the Code classifies each offence, not who shouted louder.

sections.keypoint: Ask for three things: the grounds, a lawyer, and to tell your family.

body.text: The Constitution gives an arrested person rights that start at once. They are short, and they are worth knowing by heart.
Article 5(3): a person arrested shall be informed as soon as may be of the grounds of his arrest. He shall also be allowed to consult and be defended by a lawyer of his choice.
The Criminal Procedure Code adds a right people forget. Somebody at home may be told where you are.
The Code requires the police to let an arrested person contact a relative or friend, and a lawyer of his choice.

items: Ask what offence you are being held for. You are entitled to be told.
Ask for someone at home to be told where you are.
Ask for a lawyer, by name if you have one.
Ask for the officer's name and the station you are being taken to.

body.text: When the right to a lawyer must be honoured is fought over in the courts. Police often say later. Ask anyway, ask again, and have someone write down each time you asked.

sections.keypoint: Twenty-four hours, then a Magistrate. That clock is in the Constitution, not just the Code.

body.text: The most useful number in this module is twenty-four. It is the limit on police detention without a Magistrate.
Article 5(4): a person arrested and not released shall be produced before a Magistrate within twenty-four hours, and shall not be detained further without the Magistrate's authority.
Faizal is arrested at nine on Sunday night. By nine on Monday night he must be released or taken before a Magistrate. If neither has happened, his family should be asking why.
The twenty-four hours leaves out the time needed to travel to the Magistrate. In a rural district that can matter. It is not a licence for a second night in the lock-up.

sections.keypoint: You must answer truthfully, but not a question whose answer would expose you to a charge.

body.text: People assume they must answer everything, or that they may answer nothing. Neither is the Malaysian position.
A person questioned by the police must answer truthfully. He need not answer a question whose answer would expose him to a criminal charge or a penalty.
body.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593), provisions on police statements

body.text: So your name and address are not optional. Explaining where the phone in your bag came from is a different matter.
A statement given to the police can be used later. Never sign one you have not read. If you cannot read it, say so and ask for it to be read out to you.

sections.keypoint: Write down the times afterwards — memory of a bad night is what the later argument turns on.

body.text: Whatever happens, someone should keep a note. Memory of a bad night is unreliable, and the times are what the arguments later turn on.

items: The time and place of the stop, and the time of the arrest.
What you were told, and what you asked for.
The names or numbers of the officers, and the station.
Every time a lawyer or a phone call was requested, and the answer given.

body.text: If the family cannot afford a lawyer, ask about the legal aid centre run by the Bar in the State. There is also a government legal aid scheme.

sections.keypoint: Nobody memorises their rights at eleven at night, which is why these five cards go in first.

body.text: Five cards. They are the ones to have by heart before you need them, because nobody memorises rights at eleven at night in a police station.
Then work the guided problem, which walks you through one arrest step by step. After that, the lesson From arrest to charge takes the classifications properly.

reading.where: the early chapters on arrest and on the rights of a person arrested

lessons.source: Federal Constitution Arts 5(3) and 5(4); Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593), including the First Schedule and s 28A.
lessons.verify: Read Arts 5(3) and 5(4) in a current reprint of the Federal Constitution. The rights on arrest in the Criminal Procedure Code have been amended more than once, so read s 28A in a current reprint before relying on the detail here. The case law on when access to a lawyer must be allowed is live and contested — read it in full rather than in summary.

quiz.q: When does a police stop become an arrest?
options: When the officer says the word arrest
When handcuffs are used
When you are taken into custody and are no longer free to leave
When you reach the police station
quiz.why: It turns on control, not on any form of words. Handcuffs are not needed either.
quiz.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593); arrest turns on custody and control

quiz.q: What must you be told when you are arrested?
options: The name of the investigating officer
The maximum sentence you face
Nothing at all until you are charged
The grounds of your arrest, as soon as may be
quiz.why: Article 5(3) says so. The trap is thinking the right only starts at the charge.
quiz.source: Federal Constitution Art 5(3)

quiz.q: After an arrest, who may you ask to contact?
options: A lawyer only
A lawyer of your choice, and a relative or friend
A relative only
Nobody until questioning has finished
quiz.why: Article 5(3) gives you the lawyer; the Code adds the relative or friend. Police often say later, so ask again and note the time.
quiz.source: Federal Constitution Art 5(3); Criminal Procedure Code s 28A

quiz.q: How long may the police hold you before a Magistrate must see you?
options: Forty-eight hours
Seven days
Until the investigation is finished
Twenty-four hours
quiz.why: Article 5(4). Longer needs a Magistrate's order, and travel time to the Magistrate is not counted.
quiz.source: Federal Constitution Art 5(4)

quiz.q: Must you answer a police question if the answer would expose you to a charge?
options: Yes, always
No, and you need not answer anything at all
Only if a lawyer is present
No, though you must answer other questions truthfully
quiz.why: The Code asks for truthful answers but protects you from ones that would incriminate you. Refusing to say anything at all is not the rule.
quiz.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593); the protection against self-incriminating answers

quiz.q: Arrested at nine on Sunday night, still in the lock-up at noon on Tuesday, no Magistrate seen. What is the position?
options: It is lawful because the investigation is not finished
The detention has run past the constitutional limit
It is lawful if a senior officer approved it
It is lawful for the first three days
quiz.why: Twenty-four hours is the limit without a Magistrate, and only a remand order extends it.
quiz.source: Federal Constitution Art 5(4)

lessons.plateCaption: Stopped, asked, arrested. Three different things, with different powers attached, and the difference matters at the roadside.

lessons.title: The lock-up, the charge and the first day in court
lessons.summary: Remand, the charge read out, the plea, and what bail and a surety really are — written for the family in the public gallery.

sections.keypoint: A night in the lock-up ends one of three ways, and knowing which tells you what to do next.
sections.h: Three roads out of the lock-up

body.text: A night in the lock-up ends in one of three ways. Knowing which one you are in tells you what to do next.

items: Released with no charge. Sometimes with a warning, sometimes with nothing said at all.
Released on police bail, with a date to come back to the station.
Taken before a Magistrate, who is asked to allow the police more time.

body.text: The third road is the remand hearing. It is where families most often turn up with no idea what is about to happen.

body.title: Which road you are on
body.caption: Knowing which of the three you are in tells you what to do next. Families most often arrive with no idea that the third one is about to happen.
body.alt: A question — how does the night end? — branching three ways. Released with no charge, sometimes with a warning. Released on police bail, with a date to come back to the station. Or taken before a Magistrate, who is asked to allow the police more time.
body.question: How does the night end?

branches.label: Released
branches.note: a warning, or nothing said at all

sections.keypoint: Beyond twenty-four hours needs a Magistrate's remand order, made for the investigation.

body.text: Remand means holding a person while the police investigate. After the first twenty-four hours only a Magistrate can allow it.
Detention beyond twenty-four hours needs a remand order from a Magistrate. It is made for the investigation, and for the period the Magistrate thinks fit.
The hearing is short and is often held in a small room. The investigating officer says why more time is needed. The person arrested may speak, and so may a lawyer.
Danial is nineteen and has never been arrested. The police ask for seven days. His lawyer points out that the phone has already been seized, so four days would do. The Magistrate gives four.
Nobody is deciding guilt at a remand hearing. Arguing that Danial did not do it is the wrong argument. The question is whether more detention is really needed.

sections.keypoint: A charge must give enough detail of time, place and person to be answered.

body.text: A charge is the written accusation read out in court. It is the first document in the case that truly belongs to the accused.
A charge must state the offence, with enough detail of time, place and person for the accused to know what he is answering.
body.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593), provisions on the form of charges

body.text: Theft of a mobile phone belonging to Puan Lim, at a shop on Jalan Melaka, on 3 March. That is enough. Theft of something, somewhere in Melaka, some time last year is not.
The charge is read in a language the accused understands. If it is not understood, say so before pleading, not afterwards.

sections.keypoint: Two real answers to a charge, and pleading guilty to get it over with is a decision with consequences.

body.text: Once the charge is read the court asks for a plea. There are two real answers.

items: Guilty. The court may convict at once, and the next step is sentence.
Not guilty, usually said in court as claiming trial. The prosecution must then prove the charge.

body.text: A guilty plea is not simply accepted. The court checks that the accused understands the charge and admits the facts behind it.
People plead guilty to get out of the lock-up sooner. It is the most expensive short cut in this module. A conviction stays on the record, and the sentence can be heavier than the wait.

sections.keypoint: Bailable means entitled; non-bailable means the court decides.

body.prompt: Danial's mother is told at the counter that he can come home today if she pays three thousand ringgit. What is that money?
options: A fine for what he is accused of
A payment to the police for letting him out
A deposit that comes back if he attends every date
body.reveal: The third, and the word for it is bail. It secures one thing: that Danial turns up. If you thought fine, you are in very good company.

body.text: Bail is not a fine and it is not a punishment. It is a promise to come back to court, backed by money.
For a bailable offence the accused is entitled to be released on bail. For a non-bailable offence bail is in the discretion of the court.
body.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593), First Schedule and s 388

body.text: Which one applies is looked up rather than argued. The First Schedule to the Code classifies each offence.
A surety, or penjamin, is a person who promises the court that the accused will attend. If the accused disappears, the surety can lose the money.
Bail is set at three thousand ringgit with one surety. Danial's mother signs the bond and deposits the money. If he attends every date, it comes back at the end.
Some Acts carry their own bail rules, and a few shut bail out. Check the Act the charge is brought under, not only the Code.

sections.keypoint: A criminal trial runs in the same order in a small case and a large one.

body.text: A criminal trial has an order, and it is the same order in a small case and a large one.

items: The prosecution calls its witnesses. Each one can be cross-examined by the defence.
The court then decides whether there is a case to answer. If there is not, the accused is acquitted.
If there is, the defence is called. The accused may give evidence or stay silent.
The court gives its decision. If it convicts, it hears mitigation before passing sentence.

body.text: Mitigation is the accused's chance to explain his circumstances before sentence. It is not a denial of guilt.
Dates get adjourned, often. Several mention dates before a trial is normal and is not a sign that something has gone wrong.
A mention date is a short hearing to move the case along. Nobody gives evidence at one. It is the day the court fixes the next thing to happen.
If the family cannot pay for a lawyer, ask about legal aid before the next date, not on the morning of it.

sections.keypoint: The problem puts you in the mother's position, not the lawyer's.

body.text: Five cards, then the problem question on remand and bail. It puts you in the position of the mother, not the lawyer.
After that, the lesson on bail and the shape of a criminal trial takes the same ground at a harder level.

reading.where: the chapters on remand, on charges, and on bail

lessons.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593), including s 117, s 388 and the First Schedule; Federal Constitution Art 5(4).
lessons.verify: The maximum remand periods under s 117 of the Criminal Procedure Code are graduated by the sentence the offence carries and have been amended — check the current text. Bail classification comes from the First Schedule, and a special Act may displace it, so check the Act the charge is brought under. Bail figures and court practice differ between courts; nothing here is a substitute for asking in the court itself.

quiz.q: Who can allow the police to hold a person beyond twenty-four hours?
options: A Magistrate, by a remand order
The investigating officer
The Public Prosecutor
The officer in charge of the station
quiz.why: Remand is a judicial decision under s 117. The police ask; the Magistrate decides.
quiz.source: Criminal Procedure Code s 117

quiz.q: What is the question at a remand hearing?
options: Whether the accused is guilty
Whether further detention is needed for the investigation
Whether bail should be granted
Whether the charge is properly drafted
quiz.why: Guilt is not in issue yet. Arguing innocence there wastes the one argument you have.
quiz.source: Criminal Procedure Code s 117

quiz.q: What must a charge tell the accused?
options: The likely sentence
The offence, with enough detail of time, place and person
The evidence the prosecution holds
The names of the witnesses
quiz.why: A person cannot answer a case he has not been told. A vague charge is one to raise at once.
quiz.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593); the provisions on the form of a charge

quiz.q: What does claiming trial mean?
options: Pleading not guilty, so the prosecution must prove the charge
Asking for a faster hearing
Asking to be tried in a higher court
Admitting the facts but disputing the sentence
quiz.why: It is the ordinary way a not guilty plea is described in a Malaysian court.
quiz.source: Standard Malaysian court practice; claiming trial is a plea of not guilty

quiz.q: What is a surety promising?
options: That the accused is innocent
To pay any fine the court imposes
To keep the accused at home
That the accused will attend court, with money at risk if he does not
quiz.why: Bail secures attendance. The surety's money is the security, and it comes back if the dates are kept.
quiz.source: Criminal Procedure Code (Act 593); the bail and bond provisions

quiz.q: When is bail a matter of right rather than of discretion?
options: When the accused has no record
When the accused is under twenty-one
When the offence is classified as bailable
When the police do not object
quiz.why: The First Schedule does the classifying. Non-bailable means the court has a discretion, not that bail is impossible.
quiz.source: Criminal Procedure Code, First Schedule; ss 387 and 388

lessons.plateCaption: The first appearance: a charge read out, and a decision about liberty taken long before any trial.

lessons.title: Who owns this land, and how would you know
lessons.summary: The register decides ownership in Malaysia. A land search is how an ordinary person reads it, and occupation is not the same thing as title.

sections.keypoint: Ask who owns a piece of land and most people answer with a family story.

body.text: Ask who owns a piece of land and most people answer with a story. Grandfather cleared it. The family has been there since before Merdeka.

body.prompt: Mak Cik Zainab's family has farmed the same lot for forty years. Her father cleared it, and died fifteen years ago. Nobody has been to the land office since. Who owns it today?
options: Mak Cik Zainab and her brothers and sisters
Her father, because his name is still on the register
Nobody, until a court is asked to decide
body.reveal: Her father. A man fifteen years dead is still, on paper, the owner. That is the ordinary position of a lot of family land here. If you picked the first answer you reasoned the way the village does. The law reasons from one page instead.

body.text: Malaysian land law does not answer with a story. It answers with a register, and the register is kept at the land office.

sections.keypoint: Under the Code you own land by being registered — the register is the title, not a record of it.

body.text: Every piece of registered land in Malaysia has a page in a State register. The person named on that page is the proprietor.
Under the National Land Code a person becomes the owner of land by being registered as proprietor. The register is the title, not merely evidence of it.
This arrangement is called the Torrens system. The name matters less than the habit it should give you. Before you believe anything about land, look at the register.
Mak Cik Zainab's family has farmed a lot in Kuala Selangor for forty years. The register still shows her late father as proprietor. In law the family are not the owners, whatever the village knows.

sections.keypoint: Anyone may order an official search at the district land office; you do not need a lawyer.
sections.h: How to read a land search

body.text: You do not need a lawyer to find out who owns land. Anyone may apply at the district land office for an official search of a lot.
You need the lot number and the mukim or district. The fee is small and the answer comes back on a page or two.

items: The registered proprietor, with an identity card or company number.
The lot number, the area, and the tenure — held for ever, or for a term of years.
The category of land use: agriculture, building or industry.
Any restriction in interest, which is a condition requiring State consent before a sale or a charge.
Anything registered against the land: a charge to a bank, a lease, or a caveat.

body.text: The certificate the family keeps in a biscuit tin is the issue document of title, often called the geran. It is a copy of the register page, not the ownership itself.
A search shows one day only. In a purchase a fresh search is done again just before the transfer is handed in for registration.

sections.keypoint: Long occupation does not turn an occupier into an owner of registered land.
sections.h: Living on land you do not own

body.text: Many Malaysians occupy land they hold no title to. Occupation and ownership are different things, and the Code keeps them apart.

items: A temporary occupation licence, or TOL, is yearly permission to occupy State land. It is permission, not ownership, and it can end.
A tenant rents. The landlord's name stays on the register throughout.
A family arrangement: one child lives on the land while the title stays in a parent's name.

body.text: Long occupation does not by itself give title to registered land under the National Land Code. Time alone does not turn an occupier into an owner.
This surprises people who have heard of squatter's rights in English law. That doctrine does not run against registered land here. The register decides.

Some titles carry a further limit. Malay reserved land can only be dealt with within a restricted class of buyers, under State law. Sabah and Sarawak have their own land legislation, so do not carry this lesson straight across.

body.title: Occupying and owning are different things

items: A TOL is yearly permission to occupy State land. Permission, not ownership.
A tenant rents. The landlord's name stays on the register throughout.
A family arrangement: one child lives there, the title stays in a parent's name.
Long occupation does not by itself give title to registered land.
The register names the proprietor, and the register is the title.
Ownership comes from registration under the National Land Code.
Time alone does not turn an occupier into an owner.
Squatter's rights from English law do not run against registered land here.

sections.keypoint: Signing is not owning: a dealing takes effect on registration, and until then you have contract rights.

body.text: Devi agrees to buy a terrace house in Klang. She signs the sale and purchase agreement and pays the deposit. She has not become the owner.
A dealing in registered land takes effect only when it is registered. Until then the buyer has rights under the contract, not title.
The gap between signing and registration can run for months. Almost everything that goes wrong in a land dispute happens inside that gap.

body.title: Where the danger sits in a purchase
body.caption: The gap can run for months. Almost everything that goes wrong in a land dispute happens inside it, which is why a fresh search is done just before the transfer goes in.
body.alt: Three stages. Devi signs the sale and purchase agreement and pays the deposit, which gives her rights under the contract but not title. Then a gap of months while the transfer is prepared and lodged. Then registration, at which point she becomes the proprietor.

steps.label: Sign, and pay the deposit
steps.note: rights under the contract, not title

steps.label: The gap
steps.note: often months — this is where disputes live

sections.keypoint: If there is land in your family, get the lot number and order a search.

body.text: Five cards. Then, if there is any land in your family, do the real thing. Get the lot number and order a search.
The lesson on title by registration takes the same idea further, into what happens when a registration was obtained by fraud.

reading.where: the opening chapters on the Torrens system and registration

lessons.source: National Land Code (Act 828); standard land office practice.
lessons.verify: The National Land Code was revised and its Act number should be confirmed against a current reprint. Search fees, forms and procedure are set by State land rules and differ between States — confirm with the district land office. Sabah and Sarawak have their own land legislation, so do not carry this straight across.

quiz.q: Who is the owner of registered land in Malaysia?
options: The person who has occupied it longest
The person holding the title document
The person registered as proprietor
The person who paid for it
quiz.why: The register is the title. Keeping the geran in a drawer is not ownership.
quiz.source: National Land Code (Act 828); title is by registration

quiz.q: What is the geran, the issue document of title?
options: The contract of sale
The ownership itself
A licence to occupy State land
A copy of the register page, held by the proprietor
quiz.why: It is a copy. What settles ownership is the register at the land office.
quiz.source: National Land Code (Act 828); the issue document of title is a copy of the register

quiz.q: What does a restriction in interest on a title mean?
options: The land cannot be dealt with at all
State consent is needed before the land is sold or charged
The land is reserved for agriculture
The proprietor is under eighteen
quiz.why: It is a condition written on the title. Missing it is a common way for a sale to stall.
quiz.source: National Land Code (Act 828); restrictions in interest endorsed on the title

quiz.q: A family has farmed land for forty years with no title in their name. What do they own?
options: The land, by long use
A half share of the land
A licence to remain
Nothing in law, unless the register says otherwise
quiz.why: Long occupation gives no title against the register under the Code.
quiz.source: National Land Code (Act 828); long occupation gives no title against the register

quiz.q: Devi signs a sale and purchase agreement and pays her deposit. What does she have?
options: Title to the land
A registered charge
Rights under the contract, but not title
A caveat over the land
quiz.why: A dealing takes effect on registration, and the gap before it is where the risk sits.
quiz.source: National Land Code (Act 828); a dealing takes effect on registration

lessons.plateCaption: The answer to “who owns this” is a document. A land search shows the proprietor, the charge and any caveat in one page.

lessons.title: The four papers behind a piece of land
lessons.summary: Transfer, charge, caveat, and the grandfather whose name is still on the title — what each document does, and why speed matters when a signature was forged.

sections.keypoint: Most land arguments are arguments about four documents.

body.text: Land arguments are usually arguments about four documents. A transfer, a charge, a caveat, and the paper that moves land on when somebody has died.
Each does one job. Learn what each one does, and most land problems become readable without a textbook.

body.caption: Each does one job. Learn what each one does, and most land problems become readable without a textbook.
rows: Changes the registered owner. The buyer's name replaces the seller's.
What a bank gets over the land when it lends against it.
A stop sign on the register.
The paper for a dead owner
Moves the land on when the owner has died.

sections.keypoint: A transfer passes ownership when it is registered, not when it is signed.

body.text: A sale ends with a transfer form signed by the seller and handed in at the land office. The office registers it, and the buyer's name replaces the seller's.
A transfer of registered land passes ownership when it is registered, not when it is signed.
Devi's transfer is handed in on a Monday and registered a fortnight later. She became the owner on the day of registration, not on the day she paid.
Stamp duty is paid before registration. Where the title carries a restriction in interest, State consent has to come first.

sections.keypoint: A charge is security for a debt — and Malaysian law says charge, not mortgage.

body.text: When a bank lends against land, it does not take ownership. It takes a registered security called a charge.
A charge is registered against the land as security for a debt. Malaysian law says charge, not mortgage.
The borrower stays the registered proprietor. The bank appears on the register as chargee, which is a different thing.
If the borrower defaults, the bank serves a notice. If the default is not put right, it applies for an order for sale.
The bank cannot simply take the house and move in. It has to go through the order for sale process, and the borrower can be heard in it.

sections.keypoint: A caveat is the stop sign: it freezes dealings while a claim is sorted out.

body.text: A caveat is a note entered on the register that blocks further dealings while it stands. It is the quickest protection an ordinary person has.
A private caveat may be entered by a person claiming title to the land, or a registrable interest in it, or a beneficial entitlement under a trust affecting it.
A caveat does not give you the land. It buys time by stopping anybody else being registered until the claim is sorted out.
Devi hears that her seller is trying to sell the same house to somebody else. She lodges a private caveat that afternoon. The second sale cannot be registered while it stands.
A caveat lodged without a proper claim is not free. A person who suffers loss because of it can claim compensation from the caveator.

sections.keypoint: Land in a dead person's name moves only when the distribution is registered.

body.text: This is the most common land problem in Malaysian families. It is a paperwork problem rather than a fight.
Land does not pass to the children by itself. The register keeps showing the dead person until the estate is distributed and that distribution is registered.

items: A small estate is dealt with at the Land Office, in a distribution hearing the family attends.
Where there is a will, or the estate is larger, the matter goes to court for a grant.
The order or grant is then registered against the title, and only then does the register change.

body.text: Land registered in a dead person's name moves on only when the distribution of the estate is registered against the title.
body.source: National Land Code (Act 828); Small Estates (Distribution) Act 1955

body.text: Delay is expensive. After two generations the heirs have multiplied, some have moved away, and some have died in turn. The cheapest time to do this is now.

sections.keypoint: Section 340 protects a registered title, and lists the exceptions — fraud, forgery, a void instrument.
sections.h: When a signature is not real

body.text: Sometimes a name reached the register through a forged transfer. The Code does not simply shrug at that.
A registered title is indefeasible, but s 340 sets out exceptions. Registration obtained by fraud, by forgery, or by a void instrument may be set aside.
The Federal Court in Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San restored the deferred position. The forger's transferee can be unwound. A later buyer in good faith, for value, is protected.
That is why speed matters. Once the land has moved on to an innocent buyer, the person who lost it may be left suing for money rather than getting the land back.

sections.keypoint: The problem is the family case above, with a forged transfer inside it.

body.text: Five cards, then the problem question. It is the family case above, with a forged transfer inside it.

lessons.source: National Land Code (Act 828), including s 340; Small Estates (Distribution) Act 1955; Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San [2010] 2 MLJ 1 (FC).
lessons.verify: Read s 340 of the National Land Code itself, including the proviso, in a current reprint. Confirm the current small estates procedure and the value threshold for a small estate — it is set by statute and has been raised. Confirm the citation of Tan Ying Hong in a report you can hold, and check whether anything later has qualified it.

quiz.q: When does a buyer become the registered owner?
options: When the transfer is registered
When the agreement is signed
When the price is paid in full
When the keys are handed over
quiz.why: Registration is the moment. Everything before it is contract.
quiz.source: National Land Code (Act 828); a transfer takes effect on registration

quiz.q: What does a bank get when it lends against land?
options: A registered charge, as security for the debt
Ownership of the land
A caveat over the land
A lease of the land
quiz.why: Malaysian law says charge, not mortgage, and the borrower stays the proprietor.
quiz.source: National Land Code (Act 828); the charge provisions

quiz.q: What does a private caveat do?
options: It transfers the land to the caveator
It blocks further dealings from being registered
It cancels the seller's title
It creates a charge over the land
quiz.why: It buys time; it gives no interest. Lodging one without a proper claim can cost compensation.
quiz.source: National Land Code (Act 828); the caveat provisions

quiz.q: A father dies with land in his name. What happens to the register?
options: It passes to the eldest child at once
Nothing, until the estate is distributed and the distribution registered
It passes to the widow at once
It goes back to the State
quiz.why: Land does not move by itself. The distribution has to be obtained and then registered.
quiz.source: Small Estates (Distribution) Act 1955; National Land Code (Act 828)

quiz.q: Where is a small estate usually distributed?
options: At the Sessions Court
At the Land Office, in a distribution hearing
At the National Registration Department
At the State Secretary's office
quiz.why: Small estates go through the Land Office. Larger ones, or those with a will, go to court.
quiz.source: Small Estates (Distribution) Act 1955

quiz.q: A transfer was forged. Is the person registered under it safe?
options: Yes, because the register is always conclusive
No — forgery is one of the exceptions in s 340
Yes, if a lawyer witnessed the signature
Only if the true owner objects within a year
quiz.why: The exceptions are listed. It is the later innocent buyer for value who is protected, which is why speed matters.
quiz.source: National Land Code s 340; Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San [2010] 2 MLJ 1 (FC)
